questions.stem: What is counted inside each quadrat when measuring biodiversity?

options.text: The number of different species present
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Mass is a biomass measure, not this biodiversity count.

options.text: The number of individuals of one species
options.explanation: That measures population size, not species diversity.
Cover tracks area, not species counts.

questions.stem: How many quadrats should each survey area receive?

options.text: Twenty-five in the first area only
options.explanation: Both areas need comparable sampling.

options.text: A minimum of ten quadrats per area
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
One sample cannot represent an area.

options.text: As many as time allows with no minimum
options.explanation: Ten is the stated minimum for representativeness.

questions.stem: What size does the example survey area take?

options.text: A hundred metres by a hundred metres
options.explanation: The example is far smaller.
The method states a defined example size.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which tool identifies unknown species in the quadrat?

options.explanation: It chooses coordinates, not identities.
Tapes frame the area, not the taxonomy.
A spare frame identifies nothing.

questions.stem: Why repeat the whole process in a second survey area?

options.text: So the species counts of the two areas can be compared
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Comparison, not budget, is the aim.

options.text: To verify the first area still exists
options.explanation: Existence checks are not part of sampling.
The key works regardless of area count.

questions.stem: State what the apparatus for measuring biodiversity includes.
questions.modelAnswer: The apparatus includes two tape measures, a quadrat, a random number generator and a species key.

questions.stem: State how many quadrats are sampled in each survey area.
questions.modelAnswer: Data is collected for ten quadrats in the first survey area before repeating in the second.

questions.stem: Explain why a larger species count signals higher biodiversity.
questions.modelAnswer: A larger count of different species signals higher biodiversity because more species living in the area means greater variety, which is the measure being taken.

questions.stem: Area one records 7 species per quadrat on average, area two records 3. Which holds higher biodiversity?
questions.modelAnswer: Area one holds higher biodiversity, since the larger number of different species found there is the indicator of greater biodiversity.

questions.stem: What do coordinates 4,5 instruct the student to do?

options.explanation: The pair identifies a valid position.

options.text: Place the quadrat 4 metres along the x-axis and 5 metres along the y-axis
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Coordinates position the frame, they are not counts.
Two separate axes values, not one sum.

questions.stem: What does a comparison of species counts between areas provide?

options.text: The distribution pattern of each species
options.explanation: The method states distribution is not revealed.
Biomass is not measured here.

options.text: An indicator of the biodiversity of each area
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The exact population of every species
options.explanation: Counts of species, not individuals, were taken.

questions.stem: What does the biodiversity measurement miss?

options.explanation: Species counts are exactly what it records.
Weather is not the stated gap.
Coordinates are known by design.

options.text: Both the distribution and the population size of the species
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which biotic factors shape the species counts?

options.text: Competition, predator-prey relationships and food web interactions
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Those are abiotic influences.
Frame material changes no ecology.
Timing matters little compared to the named factors.

questions.stem: Why does the student count different species rather than individuals here?

options.explanation: The quadrat number is unrelated to the choice of measure.

options.text: Because the aim is biodiversity, measured as the variety of species present
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Individuals are countable; the aim simply differs.
Keys support identification, not bans.

questions.stem: State the steps of placing the first quadrat.
questions.modelAnswer: Random coordinates are generated, and the quadrat is placed at that point, such as 4 metres along one axis and 5 along the other.

questions.stem: State what a higher average species count indicates.
questions.modelAnswer: A higher average count of different species indicates a higher level of biodiversity in that area.

questions.stem: Explain why random placement matters more than speed in this method.
questions.modelAnswer: Random placement matters more because the data must represent the survey area, and speed gained by biased spots corrupts the biodiversity estimate.

questions.stem: A student wants population size as well as biodiversity. What extra record is needed?
questions.modelAnswer: Counts of individuals per species are needed, since the species-only method reveals neither distribution nor population size.

questions.stem: In this investigation, what does the C of CORMS identify as changed?

options.explanation: Weather is not the changed variable named.
The key stays the same across areas.

options.text: The study area where data is collected
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The frame stays constant throughout.

questions.stem: Which measurement does M1 record here?

options.explanation: Height is not the recorded measurement.

options.text: The mass of soil per quadrat
options.explanation: Soil mass is not measured in this method.
Timing is not the measurement recorded.

options.text: The number of different plant species across all quadrats
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

questions.stem: Why does R matter in this evaluation?

options.text: Repeating the investigation several times ensures the results are reliable
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Reliability, not idleness, justifies repeats.

options.text: Because one quadrat is always perfect
options.explanation: Single readings are weak; repeats strengthen them.
The scientific reason is reliability of the estimate.

questions.stem: Which item belongs in the S of CORMS here?

options.explanation: Species counted belongs to O, not S.

options.text: The size of the quadrat and the random placement method
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Student count is not the named standard.

options.text: The colour of the tape measure
options.explanation: Tape colour is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Why does M2 barely apply in this scenario?

options.explanation: One measurement is actively taken.
Plants are measured fine; there is just no second measure.

options.text: Because only one kind of measurement, the species count, is taken
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Because M2 was deleted from CORMS
options.explanation: M2 simply finds no second measurement to describe.

questions.stem: State what each letter of CORMS prompts.
questions.modelAnswer: CORMS prompts the Change made, the Organism studied, the Repeats taken, the Measurements recorded and the Standards controlled.

questions.stem: State the solution for missing organisms under leaves.
questions.modelAnswer: A pencil or stick lifts the leaves out of the way so hidden organisms can be seen and counted.

questions.stem: Explain why random quadrat placement belongs under Standards in this evaluation.
questions.modelAnswer: Random placement belongs under Standards because it is held constant across both areas, keeping the sampling method identical and the comparison fair.

questions.stem: A student samples one area in morning sun and the other at dusk. Which CORMS letter flags it?
questions.modelAnswer: S flags it, because the day and conditions should be controlled, and sampling at different times breaks that standard.
